md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
md: Architecture is placement. For each trust boundary, name the enforcement point, check that nothing can go around it, and list what it depends on. Those dependencies are your trusted computing base, and they deserve the most scrutiny.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
md: Zero trust concentrates trust in the policy engine, the administrator, the identity provider and the device inventory. Protect them as the most critical systems you run, and treat a change to access policy as a security event.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: Before asking "is this secure?", ask "which asset, and which property: confidentiality, integrity or availability?" Different properties need different defences: encryption (scrambling data so only holders of a secret key can read it) mostly protects confidentiality, hashes and signatures protect integrity and authenticity, and backups and redundancy protect availability.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: The leak did not create the vulnerability; it created a free, reliable exploit. By the time WannaCry hit, the patch had existed for 59 days. Treat every critical advisory as if working exploit code will be public soon, because sometimes it already is.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Authorisation is the line. Own it or get written, scoped permission; stop at other people's data; report privately and give owners time to fix. Practise on platforms built for it.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
md: Do not copy a threshold from a tutorial or a library default. Collect a few hundred real pairs from your traffic, label whether the cached answer would be correct, and pick the threshold from that data and your cost of a wrong answer. Re-check whenever you change the embedding model, since similarity scales differ between models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
md: Validate the *destination*, not the *string*: fixed scheme, allowlisted host, resolved IP checked against private ranges, the connection pinned to that IP, and no automatic redirects. Then assume the check will one day fail and limit what the network lets the server reach.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Greedy longest-prefix-first can **starve** a request whose prefix is never cached: requests that hit keep jumping ahead of it. The paper says so directly and leaves fair cache-aware scheduling as future work. Watch tail latency (the latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile) if you enable `lpm`.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: A* is Dijkstra with key g + h. Never overestimate (admissible) and you keep optimality; satisfy the triangle inequality (consistent) and each node is settled once. The closer h is to the true remaining cost, the fewer nodes settle.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
md: Pick the filter by the job: moving average to smooth in time, windowed-sinc FIR (firwin) for clean band separation with linear phase, Butterworth IIR (as SOS) for a cheap sharp cutoff. Offline, filter forward and backward to cancel the delay.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Neon is fixed 128-bit SIMD. SVE is vector-length agnostic: 128 to 2048 bits (a power of two), chosen by the chip. Predicates from whilelt make the tail just another iteration, so one binary scales across vector lengths.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
md: slime is a thin layer: Ray places the workers, SGLang generates, Megatron trains, and slime owns the glue in between (the Data Buffer, the rollout function and weight sync). Most behavior you might want to change is a command-line flag or a function path, not a fork.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
md: Allow-listing the scanner fixes the noise but creates a blind spot: an attacker on that address is now invisible to the rule. The NCSC says allow lists must be "strongly object/time bounded" (one address, its scheduled window, an expiry date) "to minimise the risk of perpetual allow listing and the evasion of monitoring".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
md: Cloud and SaaS triage starts with three questions: what kind of credential is this, where is it being used from compared with normal, and what did it touch. The third question can only be answered if the right logs (S3 data events, the warehouse's query history) were switched on and kept long enough before the incident.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
md: IDW ignores how sensors sit relative to each other. S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart and both read 11, so they carry nearly the same information. IDW still counts both at full weight. If ten sensors sat in one parking lot, IDW would let that lot outvote everything else. Kriging, later in the course, fixes this.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
md: Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: `free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: b = 1 is not "more correct". It assumes every long document is just verbose. For collections where long documents genuinely cover more (manuals, books split into chapters), strong normalization buries them. The survey reports that values around 0.5 < b < 0.8 work well in many settings, with optimal values depending on the documents and queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based **optimizer** (the algorithm that updates the parameters during training) starts from.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Intersection is a linear merge over sorted lists. Make it cheap by starting from the rarest term, and make long lists skippable.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A null pointer or an uninitialized pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is *undefined behavior*: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. Often you get a crash (a segmentation fault on Linux: the process touched an address with no memory mapped there, so the operating system kills it), but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so do not rely on a crash to tell you.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: $(m \times n)(n \times p) = (m \times p)$. Each entry is a row-column dot product, the product means apply the right matrix first, and order matters.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Zero training error is not proof of a good model, and not proof of a bad one either. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and poor test error; lesson 5 shows that large modern networks can also hit zero training error and still generalize.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
md: A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
md: Clipping must go **after** `loss.backward()`, which computes the gradients, and **before** `optimizer.step()`, which applies the update. Andrej Karpathy (his training recipe is lesson 5) keeps a list of silent bugs that includes clipping the *loss* instead of the gradients, which simply ignores outlier examples instead of taming their updates.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
md: Verifying 'signed by somebody' proves nothing: an attacker can get a valid Sigstore certificate for their own identity in seconds. The security comes from `--certificate-identity` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer`, which you must set to the one workflow or person you actually expect.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent (one gradient step per token, in arrival order) on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
md: Default deny, check every request in one place, keep that place small, and assume the attacker has read the code. Most broken access control bugs violate at least one of these four.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: The padlock icon means "this connection is encrypted to the named site", not "this site is safe". Phishing sites get valid certificates for their own domains in seconds.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
md: mTLS answers "which service is calling?". It does not answer "is this service allowed to do this?". Authorization (orders may charge, but not refund) is still your application's job, keyed on the verified identity.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, which give a process its own view of process ids, mounts and network, and cgroups, control groups that cap its CPU, memory and I/O). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
md: SIMD kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar loop. FAISS explicitly allows reassociation in its distance loops; that is a deliberate choice, not a bug. Do not assert exact equality of distances across CPUs or builds.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
md: Do not read `world_size` as the data-parallel size. On 8 GPUs with TP 2 a WorkerGroup has 8 workers but only 4 data shards. Splitting the batch 8 ways would hand different samples to two GPUs that must run the same sharded matmul together.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
md: pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
md: A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the image at full resolution. It sees whatever grid the encoder produced. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo squeezed into 336 x 336 loses most of its pixels before the language model ever runs.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
md: The progress ladder, weakest to strongest: **blocking** (a stalled lock holder can stop everyone), **lock-free** (some thread always completes), **wait-free** (every thread completes in finitely many of its own steps), **bounded wait-free** (every thread completes within a fixed number of its own steps).

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: An MLWP model learns one function: global state now (a tensor of about 10^8 numbers) to global state a few hours later, supervised by reanalysis.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
md: The same-origin policy limits what a page can **read** from other origins. It does not stop a page from **sending** requests to them, and it does nothing at all to code that is already running inside your origin. State-changing endpoints need their own protection on the server.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
md: Windows security is identity attached to processes. A process acts with the token it was given, so "which account ran this, and with which token" is the first question in almost every Windows investigation.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Patch Tuesday and PrintNightmare: closing holes on a schedule
md: Attack surface reduction: every service running as SYSTEM is a door. If a machine does not need a service (printing on a domain controller, SMBv1 anywhere, RDP on the internet), turn it off. You cannot be exploited through code that is not running.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Bluetooth and BLE: pairing, KNOB and BlueBorne
md: Bluetooth has two separate risk classes. Protocol design (pairing models, KNOB's unauthenticated negotiation) decides what a nearby listener or MITM can do to a correct implementation. Implementation bugs (BlueBorne) let a nearby attacker run code, with no pairing at all. Updates fix both; turning Bluetooth off removes the second.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
md: In a zero-shot classifier, the label text plays the role of the trained weights. Changing a label's wording changes the classifier, so wording, templates, and descriptions are design decisions you test, not decoration.
